stops.name: Balkh, the house of Baha al-Din Walad
stops.campa: In the merchant city of Balkh, gate of Khorasan, a son is born to Baha al-Din Walad, the preacher known through the province as Sultan al-Ulama, Sultan of the Scholars, whose sermons on the soul's encounter with God fill the great mosque past its doors. They name him Muhammad, called Jalal al-Din: Glory of the Faith. The house stands among gardens and canals under the shadow of the old citadel; scholars, dervishes and the sons of emirs pass daily through its rooms. No one yet says what the astrologers will later claim they saw written in his nativity.

stops.name: Balkh, the Sultan of the Scholars and the philosophers' enmity
stops.campa: The boy grows in a house at war with the fashion of the age. Baha al-Din Walad thunders from the pulpit against the rationalist philosophers favored at the Khwarazmshah's court, calling their proofs a cage built around God; the court philosophers name him back a vulgar preacher and worse. Years of standing enmity gather over the family like weather. Baha al-Din begins to speak of departure, of a world about to be poured out like a cup — though what is truly gathering beyond the Oxus, in the felt tents of the Mongol camps, no one in Balkh has yet named.

stops.name: Balkh, the dream that empties the city
stops.campa: In the year the world tips, Baha al-Din Walad gathers his household, his books, and the small son not yet twelve, and takes the western road. The tradition remembers a dream sent before the going out: the ground of Balkh opening like a sea, the whole standing world afloat and sinking. Within two years the actual sea will come: Genghis Khan's armies will break the city's walls, slaughter its people, and burn what the family left behind. Baha al-Din does not wait to see it. The caravan turns its face toward Nishapur, and behind it Balkh keeps counting down its years.

stops.name: Nishapur, blessed by Attar
stops.campa: In Nishapur, city of the perfumers and the poets, the caravan halts and the old sheikh Farid al-Din Attar receives them. He sees the father walking ahead of the small son and says the sentence the tradition will not let go: here comes a sea followed by an ocean. He calls the boy aside, puts into his hands his own book of the soul's entanglement in the world, the Asrarnama, the Book of Secrets, and tells those standing near that this child will soon set fire to the hearts of the world's lovers. Two years later the Mongols will take Attar's own life in this same city.
stops.quote: Here comes a sea followed by an ocean.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Farid al-Din Attar on receiving the family at Nishapur (Dowlatshah, Tadhkirat al-Shu'ara; Aflaki, Manaqib al-'Arifin)

stops.name: Baghdad, thirty days at the tomb of Junayd
stops.campa: The road west brings the family to Baghdad, seat of the Caliphate, city of a thousand years of the science of hearts. Baha al-Din will not lodge in the khanqahs of the great sheikhs, saying he has no need of any teacher but the one within; but he permits the household a month's rest, and the boy is taken to pray at the tombs of the old masters of the Sufi path, Junayd and Ma'ruf al-Karkhi among them, whose sayings on annihilation in God he will echo, unknowing, in verses not yet written. The caravan turns south, toward the House of God.

stops.name: Mecca, the circling of the Kaaba
stops.campa: Baha al-Din Walad leads his household through the desert to perform the Hajj, the duty owed once in a life. The boy who will one day write that the lovers of God have a Kaaba of their own, built of the heart and needing no stone, circles here the actual House, the black corner-stone, the well of Zamzam, among the thousands of the pilgrimage year. Whatever is later made of it in verse, the canon insists the actual dust of Mecca is under his feet this once: the outward rite performed in full before the inward one is ever spoken of.

stops.name: Damascus, the child before Ibn al-Arabi
stops.campa: Returning north from the pilgrimage the family rests in Damascus, city of jasmine and the Umayyad minarets. The tradition preserves one meeting here that later ages will marvel at: the great Shaykh al-Akbar, Muhyi al-Din Ibn al-Arabi, watches Baha al-Din Walad cross a courtyard with his son a pace behind, and says to those beside him, in wonder, praise be to God, an ocean walking behind a lake. Neither master nor boy yet knows what the boy will become; the sentence is set down anyway, waiting, like the Asrarnama, for its own fulfillment.
stops.quote: Praise be to God! An ocean walking behind a lake!
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Ibn al-Arabi on seeing the boy Rumi behind his father in Damascus (later Mevlevi hagiographic tradition)

stops.name: Malatya, the bread of exile
stops.campa: Word comes that the Mongols have taken Samarkand and are pouring into Khorasan; the family does not turn back. They cross into Anatolian lands under Seljuk rule, safe for now behind the Taurus passes, and settle for a time in Malatya, an Armenian and Turkish town of weavers and copper-smiths on the old caravan road. Baha al-Din teaches; the boy studies grammar, law, and the Qur'an at his father's knee and among his father's students. Refugees from the eastern provinces keep arriving with worse news each season: Balkh fallen, Nishapur fallen, Attar himself among the dead of that second city.

stops.name: Erzincan, the patronage of the Malika Ismati Khatun
stops.campa: From Malatya the family moves to Erzincan, called to the court of the Malika Ismati Khatun, wife of the Mengujekid ruler, who has heard of the wandering scholar's fame and builds him a madrasa in her city. For a season the family knows a settled roof and a princely patron; Baha al-Din completes pages of his Ma'arif here, dictating the visions and spiritual states that will one day astonish his son when he finds the manuscript again in Konya and reads his dead father's inner life for the first time, weeping over sentences he had never been told.

stops.name: Larende (Karaman), seven years, the marriage to Gowhar Khatun
stops.campa: The family settles longest at Larende, the town later ages will call Karaman, where Baha al-Din is given a post at last with some permanence. Here the wandering pauses seven years, long enough for the boy to become a young man formed equally in law and in longing. On his father's arrangement he marries Gowhar Khatun, daughter of a fellow exile from Samarkand, Sharaf al-Din Lala; the wedding is kept in the plain style of scholars, without the ceremony a court would have given a Sultan of the Learned's son. The road that carried him from Balkh finally sets down, for a while, a household.

stops.name: Larende, the birth of Sultan Walad
stops.campa: A son is born to Jalal al-Din and Gowhar Khatun and named Baha al-Din Muhammad after his grandfather, though the world will remember him by his title, Sultan Walad: he will grow to be his father's first biographer, the keeper of the Shams story in his own Persian verse, and, when the turning founds itself into an order after his father's death, its true architect. A second son, Ala al-Din Muhammad, will follow within a few years. In this small provincial house at Larende, without any of the parties knowing it, the whole future government of the Mevlevi order is already asleep in its cradle.

stops.name: Konya, arrival at the sultan's invitation
stops.campa: The Seljuk sultan of Rum, Ala al-Din Kayqubad, builder-king of a capital he means to make the ornament of Anatolia, invites the renowned Sultan of the Learned to his city and grants the family a madrasa of their own. Konya receives them: a walled city of blue-tiled minarets under the shadow of Alaeddin Hill, crossed by trade roads from Iran, Syria and the Byzantine coast, thick with jurists, poets and dervishes of every stripe. Baha al-Din takes up his last post here. Jalal al-Din, twenty-two years old, does not yet know that every remaining stone of his life will be laid in this one city.
